South America

Stocks

Immigrants in each country, 1995–2022

Both maps show the same thing, people born in another country living in each country on 1 January of each year, and change the unit. Share: for every hundred residents, how many were born in another country. People: the total, without subtracting those who emigrated, so it is a gross stock and not a net balance. Move the year slider or press ▶ to see the evolution; the colour scale is the same across all years.

Reading. Between 1995 and 2022 the biggest jump was Chile, from 1.2 to 7.6 per cent: from one in eighty-five residents to one in thirteen. Colombia rose from 0.3 to 3.7 per cent. Argentina stayed close to where it was, from 4.5 to 3.8 per cent, though in absolute terms it gained 154,184 people. * Values come from a modelled estimate rather than a census record, so they may differ from national censuses. In Argentina the 2022 census counts 1,933,463 people born abroad against 1,746,798 in this series, 10.7 per cent more.

Reading. In 1995 the largest stock was Argentina, with 1,592,614 people born in another country. By 2022 only Colombia had overtaken it, with 1,923,421; Argentina remained second with 1,746,798. The fastest jump was Chile, from 169,404 to 1,484,654: it multiplied by 9 without reaching it. * Values come from a modelled estimate rather than a census record, so they may differ from national censuses. In Argentina the 2022 census counts 1,933,463 people born abroad against 1,746,798 in this series, 10.7 per cent more.

Source. Gaskin, T. & Abel, G. J. (2026). Deep learning four decades of human migration. Nature. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10611-7. Stock by country of birth (stock_mean), as of 1 January.

Flows between the countries of the region

All corridors between countries

Average annual flow in the period for each origin (row) → destination (column) pair. Logarithmic colour scale; k = thousands, M = millions. Mobility up to 2022 and only corridors with data.

Reading. Between 1995 and 2002, the largest corridor was Colombia → Venezuela, with 20,228 people per year on average.

Reading. Between 2003 and 2014, the largest corridor was Colombia → Venezuela, with 44,764 people per year on average.

Reading. Between 2015 and 2023, the largest corridor was Venezuela → Colombia, with 372,033 people per year on average.

Reading. Between 1995 and 2002, the largest corridor was Argentina → Brazil, with 2,607,421 trips per year on average.

Reading. Between 2003 and 2014, the largest corridor was Argentina → Brazil, with 2,781,344 trips per year on average.

Reading. Between 2015 and 2022, the largest corridor was Argentina → Paraguay, with 4,202,704 trips per year on average.

Sources. Gaskin, T. & Abel, G. J. (2026). Deep learning four decades of human migration. Nature. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10611-7. Annual flow by country of previous residence (mig_prev). Grohmann, T., Recchi, E. & Bernasconi, L. (2025). The 10 Billion Travel World: Continuity and Change in Global Transnational Mobility (1995–2022). Global Transnational Mobility Dataset (GTMD2). International visitors (gtmd2_vflow_int); corridors without data are not added.

The South American system in three periods

Each circle shows the twelve South American countries among themselves, with flows in both directions: each ribbon takes the colour of its origin country. The scale is the same across the three periods of each series, so growth shows as the ring filling up rather than circles changing size. Threshold: none, every corridor with flow is drawn.

Reading. In 1995–2002 the largest corridor in the region was Colombia → Venezuela, with 161,823 person-years. By 2015–2023 the same pair had reversed and Venezuela → Colombia reached 3,348,298: flows touching Venezuela went from 27.7% of the regional system to 68.9%.

Reading. Mobility draws a different system. The largest corridor in 1995–2002 was Argentina → Brazil and in 2015–2023 Argentina → Paraguay; flows touching Venezuela are only 3.3% of the total, because most of it is visitors between Argentina, Brazil and Chile.

Sources. Gaskin, T. & Abel, G. J. (2026). Deep learning four decades of human migration. Nature. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10611-7. Annual flow by country of previous residence (mig_prev). Grohmann, T., Recchi, E. & Bernasconi, L. (2025). The 10 Billion Travel World: Continuity and Change in Global Transnational Mobility (1995–2022). Global Transnational Mobility Dataset (GTMD2). International visitors (gtmd2_vflow_int); corridors without data are not added.

Annual sum of flows with origin or destination in a country of South America: between countries of the region, with the rest of the Americas, or with the rest of the world (both directions).

Reading. 23% of migration involving South America took place within the region in 1995, and 56% in 2019.

Reading. 64% of trips involving South America took place within the region in 1995, and 60% in 2019.

Net migration of each country

People arriving in the country from any other country minus people leaving it for any other country. Blue: more arrive than leave; red: the opposite.

Reading. Between 2015 and 2021, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay had a positive net balance. Each panel has its own scale.

Source. Gaskin, T. & Abel, G. J. (2026). Deep learning four decades of human migration. Nature. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10611-7. Annual flow by country of previous residence (mig_prev).

The grey band in the charts marks 2022–2023, years in which the data may be distorted by the Gaskin and Abel model adjustment.

In the Venezuelan case, the 2018 and 2019 flows cannot be separated precisely. The model estimates the stock at 1 January of each year and the flow is the difference between two consecutive years, so in reality the jump may be spread across both. The size and direction of the change do not depend on that assignment.
